books.section: Topic 7.4 The Progressives — The Jungle and the Meat-packing Industry
The Progressive Era and World War I (1900-1920)

stimulus.source_note: Verbatim excerpt (abridged) from the Federal Meat Inspection Act, 1906, public domain.
stimulus.text: For the purposes hereinbefore set forth the Secretary shall cause to be made, by inspectors appointed for that purpose, an examination and inspection of all cattle, sheep, swine, and goats before they shall be allowed to enter into any slaughtering, packing, or canning establishment... and said inspectors shall have access at all times, by day or night, whether the establishment be operated or not, to every part of said establishment; and said inspectors shall mark, stamp, tag, or label as 'Inspected and passed' all such products found to be not adulterated. — Federal Meat Inspection Act, 1906 (abridged)

source: original; stimulus paraphrased from 5 Steps to a 5 2024, Chapter 20, and Barron's Premium 2027, Chapter 9
stem: Supporters of the act had goals most similar to supporters of

options.text: the Federal Aid Highway Act of 1956 that built interstate highways
options.misconception: The highway act built roads; it did not protect consumers from dangerous products.

options.text: the Airline Deregulation Act of 1978 that removed airline rules
options.misconception: Deregulation removed government rules; the meat act added them, so the goals point opposite ways.

options.text: later consumer-protection laws such as the Consumer Product Safety Act of 1972
the Smoot-Hawley Tariff of 1930 that raised import taxes
options.misconception: Smoot-Hawley raised tariffs to protect American producers, not to protect consumers from unsafe goods.

rationales.A: Highways moved cars, not consumer safety. The meat act protected buyers from adulterated food.
rationales.B: Deregulation took government rules away. The meat act added federal inspection, the opposite direction.
rationales.C: Both the meat act and later consumer-protection laws used federal power to shield buyers from products that could harm them. The goal is the same: safe goods, enforced by inspection and standards.
rationales.D: Smoot-Hawley protected producers with high tariffs. The meat act protected consumers with inspection.
rationales.general:
1. Name the act's goal. Protect Americans from adulterated meat by inspecting it before sale.
2. Find the same goal later. The Consumer Product Safety Act of 1972 also used federal power to keep dangerous products from consumers.
3. Rule out the unlike cases. Highways, deregulation, and tariffs served other goals entirely.
Remember: laws resemble each other by goal, not by date, so compare what each law is trying to protect.
